canonical_title: A Dark-Haired Girl & PKD: Letters from the Heart, the Spleen, and the Funnybone
author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: This fifty-one-page collection, compiled and edited by Linda Castellani (Linda Levy) in 2008, presents her personal correspondence with Philip K.
page_summary:
This fifty-one-page collection, compiled and edited by Linda Castellani (Linda Levy) in 2008, presents her personal correspondence with Philip K. Dick, one of the women he described as one of his 'dark-haired girls.' Castellani structures the letters into sections labeled 'PKD, Side One' through 'PKD, Side Four' plus 'Odds and Ends,' each shown with one page partially obscured by puzzle-piece imagery she says was chosen to reflect 'the puzzle that was the man himself.' Beyond the letters, the volume includes her personal copy of The Dark-Haired Girl, two pencil-signed Georg Grosz prints, the only known prints of three photographs Dick took of her, and a November 1975 Rolling Stone issue containing a Dick profile that he sent her a dollar to buy. Castellani frames Dick as genuinely multidimensional -- capable of love, longing, playfulness, and humor, but also meanness, vindictiveness, and a brooding darkness she says led to outbursts of physical and emotional violence toward women he professed to love -- and cites a December 1972 letter from Dick to Roger Zelazny describing his search for 'the dark-haired girl' and mentioning 127 pages of letters to his agent compiled as a journal originally titled 'The Dark-Haired Girl: A Search for the Authentic Human Being.'

**Why it matters.** This self-published collection is a valuable, if non-scholarly, primary-source window into one of Dick's real-life romantic entanglements with the recurring 'dark-haired girl' figure that appears throughout his fiction and his own self-mythologizing correspondence (notably his December 1972 letter to Roger Zelazny). Because it is compiled and framed entirely by the recipient rather than through independent editorial verification, its characterizations of Dick -- both sympathetic and critical -- should be read as one participant's testimony rather than as adjudicated biographical fact.

*Castellani's explicit motive for publishing -- getting her account into print before a Paul Giamatti biopic then in development could fix a different public image of Dick -- frames the entire collection as an act of personal historical intervention as much as archival preservation.*

critical_caution: This is a fan-compiled and self-published memoir/letters collection by Linda Levy (writing as Linda Castellani), not a scholarly or major-press edition. Its framing of Dick's character, including claims about violence toward women, is Castellani's own account and should be read as one participant's testimony rather than adjudicated fact.
